newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds firm, curve continues to steepen.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds firm, curve continues to steepen.

text.p: Irish government bonds continued to firm in active late afternoon trade on Friday and the Irish yield curve continued to steepen, dealers said.

"The market has been very firm today. We have seen more curve steepening. In fact, this week in the Irish market the curve has actually steepened by a huge 30 basis points which is quite historical," Riada's Padraic Garvey said.

"The rally of this week was led by the short-end and that in turn reflected the fact that the punt was very strong against the mark and the fact that the money markets were very liquid which pushed down interbank rates," he added.
Garvey said that the market might be expected to top off, particularly at the short-end, in next week's trade.
"We feel that the market has not paid due regard to the Irish credit numbers and to the evidence from the Exchequer Borrowing Returns that the economy is booming," Garvey said.
"It is something that the Irish Central Bank is very aware of for they have been in trying to hold up the one-month money market rate, which they have done," he added.
Garvey said the net effect of foreign buying was to push liquidity into the Irish market and push up the punt which drives money-market rates down.

"That has left us with two competing elements and for the moment the liquidity effect is winning. That is causing the Irish curve to steepen and causing the short-end to out-perform creating very bullish conditions all round," he said.

By 1545 GMT, the 8.00 percent bond due 2000 had risen 35p from Thursday's close to 107.40 to yield 5.80 percent while the 8.00 percent bond due 2006 had risen 45p on the day to 108.30 to yield 6.70 percent.
The key one-month money market rate was at 5.56/5.68 compared to 5.50/.62 at Thursday's close.
Garvey said the market was very much divided on whether or not a cut in Irish interest rates was likely over the short-term.
"There was in effect a rate cut today with the Irish Permanent cutting its three-year and five-year fixed mortgage rates by 50 basis points," said Garvey.

"Central Bank is likely to do everything in their power to prevent a cut in variable (mortgage) interest rates...but if the current situation does not change over the next week or so then the pressure will be on for something to be done," he added.
